Gaming_Tech.title: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit
Gaming_Tech.text:
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".

The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.

The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.

Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.

Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.

The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.

Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.

They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."

The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.

"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said.

"And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."

Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.

Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".

Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".

But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord.

Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.

It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.

The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said.

"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight over the technology.

On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.

The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.

Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".

The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.

Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.

During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".

Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.

With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.

But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

Gaming_Tech.title: Regulating AI 'not the right place to start' says Bank of England governor
Gaming_Tech.text:
The Governor of the Bank of England has said regulating artificial intelligence (AI) "is not the right place to start" but instead called first for "rigorous" testing to find vulnerabilities and create safeguards to contain risk.

Writing his first-ever article for Substack, Andrew Bailey said the risks around AI were "real and increasingly significant".

He said AI development should not be halted or prohibited - "on the contrary, the benefits are immense" - but added there must be a system for intervention and to establish boundaries in which AI operates.

The debate about the potential risks surrounding the rapid development of AI and what it means for humanity has intensified in recent weeks.

The bosses of leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI have called for development of the technology to slow down and for an internationally co-ordinated approach assessing risks and putting safeguards in place.

OpenAI recently announced that it would not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

The idea of a slowdown, however, has been rejected by the likes of President Donald Trump who has said the US is leading the AI race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

Gaming_Tech.title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
Gaming_Tech.text:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.

The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.

In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".

He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.

"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.

"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."

The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.

According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.

The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.

Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.

Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.

And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.

"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.

The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.

In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.

It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.

WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.

Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
Gaming_Tech.text:
OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots", a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant it says can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf.

At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of."

At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions.

Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives.

The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of."

A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children.

Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously.

"You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added.

At the event, Altman reiterated his decision for OpenAI to not make a highly anticipated stock market debut until it can "make confident safety decisions".

The company has been preparing for a blockbuster listing, potentially valuing the firm at up to $1.4tn (£1.06tn).

Altman told reporters that "it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety, security stay well ahead of capabilities."

OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves.

He also said they had discussed creating a ten-person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing"

Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public.

"We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday.

"I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders.

Gaming_Tech.title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
Gaming_Tech.text:
Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.

Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.

It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.

Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".

The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.

Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning.

"Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.

Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.

These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.

While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.

Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.

Mindgard has not proven whether the answers supplied by Kimi on concerning topics would work.

But it argued guardrails should have prevented the models in question from entering into discussion with users on such subjects.

The firm said it was also confident a jailbroken Kimi 2.6 could allow hackers to run code on its computing resources and connect to the internet - making it a potential launchpad for cyber-attacks.

Garraghan defended Mindgard's decision to publicly discuss its jailbreak of Moonshot's systems, saying it had informed the developer and was not revealing key details about how it got the firm's models to ignore guardrails.

Mindgard alerted Moonshot to the jailbreak in an email on 27 July, following up about a week later.

It then published a blog about the issue on 12 September.

But the company said Moonshot only made contact recently, after it was approached by the BBC for comment.

In part of an email to Mindgard asking for more details, shared with the BBC by Moonshot, it said its model had generally shown "a high refusal rate for these types of requests" in internal evaluations.

Gaming_Tech.title: The start-ups hoping to return battery making to the US
Gaming_Tech.text:
As heatwaves scorched Europe this summer, workers at a US battery company noticed an uptick in demand.

San Diego-based Unigrid sells a nine kilowatt hour battery for people's homes. Sweltering European homeowners were apparently looking for ways of storing power when it was available from the grid at lower rates. They could then run air conditioners more cheaply, off the battery, during the worst heat of the day.

"We have requests coming from Spain, France, Germany, The Netherlands," says Darren Tan, co-founder and chief executive. "We've shipped the first 100 units and [expect to ship] 1,000 before the end of the year."

Unigrid's battery is an emerging technology – it's a sodium ion, rather than lithium ion device. Sodium ion batteries have got energy storage experts excited because they could end up much cheaper to build and operate than lithium ion.

They're potentially less likely to catch fire and should also work in a wider range of temperatures, even down to lows of minus 40C, external.

But there's a debate over what constitutes the best, and safest, sodium ion battery design. Plus, more than one, external US company working in this space has floundered in recent years, external.

China leads the world in sodium ion battery manufacturing at present so US competitors are going to have to work hard to keep up.

The prize that awaits is the possibility of batteries made in the US with 100% US-sourced materials. This is unlike lithium ion batteries, where China dominates the materials, external supply chain as well as manufacturing.

For Tan, China has helped his company get to market. The Unigrid battery currently uses sodium ion cells made there, rather than in the US. "We can switch back and forth and choose what battery we want to work with," says Tan, explaining that, in future, his firm might source cells from the US – though these may come at a different cost.

There's another consideration. Unigrid's battery contains chromium-3 in its cathode. In a battery, electrons flow from cathode to anode, external when charging and in the opposite direction when discharging or providing power.

Prof Dame Clare Grey at the University of Cambridge, who is co-founder of battery firm Nyobolt, points out that under certain conditions chromium-3 may form chromium-6, a toxic, cancer-causing material., external

"If you're going to go for sodium […] and you're going to sell safety, then don't start putting elements in that are going to raise red flags," she tells the BBC.

Ivana Hasa, at the Warwick Manufacturing Group, University of Warwick, who has no connection to Unigrid, agrees that it is possible for chromium-3 to form chromium-6 at very high states of charge, though she says this can be mitigated by how voltage is controlled within the battery. "Safety tests reported on the cell chemistry are very promising," she says of Unigrid's tech.

Tan says concerns around toxicity of the battery's materials are "overblown" and emphasises that Unigrid's battery has passed certification and safety tests for sale in Europe and is currently undergoing such evaluations for the US market.

Third-party tests have not been able to get the battery to form chromium-6, he says. "We've tried very hard to try and produce it, we've overcharged it as much as we can... We were unsuccessful in generating chromium-6."

The choice of cathode material, or how the electrolyte – which separates cathode and anode – is formulated are key details influencing the performance and longevity of sodium ion batteries. Some manufacturers are not using chromium for their cathode but hard carbon instead, or sodium iron phosphate pyrophosphate (NFPP).

In general, confidence around sodium ion batteries' reliability has increased during the last few years, says Prof Dame Grey, meaning they are now finding their way into grid storage applications.

Last December, LFP batteries – a relatively cheap form of lithium ion battery – were trading at $81 per kilowatt hour, external (kWh) whereas Unigrid's sodium ion battery pricing is roughly $100 kWh, external.

Some companies that spoke to the BBC suggested sodium ion might reach as low as $30 per kWh but analysts say significantly lower costs could be many years away, external.

Sodium ion batteries are also not as energy dense as lithium ion batteries, meaning they must be slightly bigger and heavier in order to provide the same amount of power.

The technology has been improving, external on this front in recent years but, even so, you're not likely to see sodium ion cells in small, energy hungry devices such as smartphones. Larger energy storage solutions are where most people expect sodium ion to dominate.

Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI scraps rollout of new AI model over safety concerns
Gaming_Tech.text:
OpenAI has announced it will not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

Its GPT-6.1 Astra system, which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself, "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, according to Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.

The ChatGPT-maker also issued an update on incidents that occurred in June but were not made public until last week, where its models accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorisation.

It comes as breaches by major AI firms' models intensify the debate about risks posed by the tech - with Anthropic underlining its concerns AI might threaten humanity as it prepares to go public.

Reuters reported on Tuesday that the AI developer - which makes ChatGPT-rival Claude - plans to warn potential investors in its Initial Public Offering (IPO) that the tech may pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity", according to a prospectus it has seen, external.

Despite the stark warnings, the company is expected to become one of the most valuable in the world when it goes public.

"I think it's kind of crazy that companies are continuing to push forward with developing these capabilities when we've already seen over the last couple of months of incidents that they're nowhere near safe and controlled enough", said Jess Whittlestone, a senior advisor on AI policy for the Centre for Long-Term Resilience think tank.

Top AI leaders including Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman have urged the industry to slow the pace of development.

OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns.

The model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added.

The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets".

OpenAI is set to hold its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, where it is expected to make several announcements. It is unclear if a new version of Astra will be among them.

The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology.

It is not the first time a large AI developer has pulled or held back a new model.

Earlier this year, Anthropic said it would not publicly release a powerful Claude model, Mythos, because it was too good at finding dormant software bugs.

The company released a version of that model to the public several months later.

OpenAI meanwhile said in 2019 it would not be "too dangerous" to release one of its GPT models, now used to power its tools like ChatGPT.

The firm's decision to not publicly release the latest version of Astra was "a welcome sign that they are taking safety concerns seriously," said Prof Tony Cohn, foundational models theme lead at the Alan Turing Institute.

But he added that "safety should not be left purely in the hands of the developers: it should also be monitored and verified through independent government-approved regulators".

Prof Gina Neff, of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, said OpenAI's announcement showed "how much more the company needs to do to make their AI products safe".

She told the BBC it was "critical" to have independent tests of AI models by labs like the UK's AI Security Institute - which evaluates frontier systems on a voluntary basis - because "these companies have proven that we can't rely solely on them for our safety".

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into government websites and systems in June in what experts said was the first known case of its kind in the world.

Albanese criticised OpenAI for notifying the Australian government through a generic email address rather than making direct contact with officials.

OpenAI said in a statement on Tuesday that it was sorry for the incident and that it "should have handled our response better".

Services Australia, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare were all affected, OpenAI clarified.

The firm said it launched investigations as soon as it became aware of issues in mid-August and notified the affected organisations between 10 and 24 September.

"Our aim was to give affected agencies a detailed account once our investigation was complete," OpenAI said, adding that it should have shared early findings more promptly and kept Australian authorities updated.

The pontiff, who said on Monday during a visit to France that AI "should be taken seriously", added he had read that Huang had suggested there could be a way to insert guardrails ‌into certain AI models.

"He's the same one, however, ⁠that says there should ⁠be no limits placed and no government regulation," said the Pope.

Nvidia declined to comment on the record.

US President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are set to host tech executives at the White House later on Tuesday to discuss regulations around AI.

Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks as a "hoax", arguing that the US has sufficient laws in place and that the only "guardrails" the technology needs is a "strong and smart" president.

Gaming_Tech.title: Apple ordered to pay $5.7bn in haptic tech patent case
Gaming_Tech.text:
Apple has been ordered to pay $5.7bn (£4.3bn) in damages after a US jury found it had used another firm's tech without permission.

Audio firm Taction Technology claimed in 2021 that Apple had infringed two of its patents for haptics systems, which enable vibrations for actions such as receiving a message or pressing a button.

This tech is built into devices like the iPhone and Apple Watch.

Apple said it had not used Taction's vibration tech and would appeal the verdict.

"While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts," it said.

"Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial."

Haptics allow people to interact with devices by simulating the sense of touch or feel through vibrations.

They have become a hallmark of modern devices, with smartphones, watches and video game controllers among those containing small motors that move in response to specific electronic signals.

Gaming_Tech.title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
Gaming_Tech.text:
The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage.

Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”.

That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets.

The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks.

The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.

In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.”

But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene.

“In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said.

However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.”

A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth.

But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”.

“Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own. The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.”

Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026.

That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit.

“The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said.

“The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

Gaming_Tech.title: Reanimated AI Greta Garbo stars again … in a ball-bearing advert
Gaming_Tech.text:
She shimmered in Hollywood’s silent movie era and lit up the first talkies – now Greta Garbo may be about to star in cinema’s new AI age.

More than a century after her screen debut and decades after her ashes were laid to rest in a Swedish woodland cemetery, the Hollywood superstar’s descendants are ready to consider an AI version of her taking a 21st-century film role.

Her likeness has already been reanimated for an advert for a Swedish industrial company, using AI generation technology. The practice some critics call “ghostploitation” has also been used in the case of the actor Val Kilmer, who died last year.

Asked if the AI Garbo could be cast in other roles, Craig Reisfield, one of three relatives who manage her legacy, told the Guardian: “I won’t say no, especially having seen what I’ve seen. It’s pretty incredible and lifelike. So what’s to say that you can’t bring Greta Garbo back in some kind of fashion in a film role?”

Reisfield said he was “flabbergasted” when he saw the AI version of his great-aunt created for publicity for the ball-bearings giant SKF. The connection comes because Garbo’s second-ever screen role was in a 1921 promotional film involving the Gothenburg-based company.

While Garbo was the definition of glamour in Hollywood’s golden age, appearing as a famous ballerina in Grand Hotel (1932) and as a doomed courtesan in Camille (1936), the 99-second AI performance for SKF is intercut with shots of ball-bearings.

However, the quality of the AI production has prompted the possibility, at least, of a greater digital comeback.

“I was totally impressed: the mannerisms that they could capture and manipulate, her dress, facial images and even her voice,” said Reisfield, a Swedish-American who used to drive for Garbo and saw her often for family occasions when she lived in New York.

“It was startling what they could do and very impactful. And it was touching, from my perspective having known her.”

A far cry from the hand-cranked cameras that captured Garbo’s early work, the SKF performance was conjured by humans prompting AI models including China’s Seedream and Google’s Nano Banana Pro.

Unusually for AI film-making, the creators did not feed moving or still images of Garbo into the AI because the material was protected by copyright. Instead, they used text prompts to create her likeness, including her ice-blue eyes and wavy blond bob. A human actor then played her role with her AI-generated appearance overlaid. Her voice was recreated from a recording from an early film.

The resulting version of Garbo appears to have gone beyond the “uncanny valley” – the problem for AI film-makers in which the closer to an actual likeness an AI rendering becomes, the more strangely implausible it seems.

AI Garbo’s lines, however, are not perhaps quite up to the standards of those given to her by MGM studio writers. At one point, she sounds like Liz Truss complaining about the “disgrace” of Britain’s cheese imports, when she says “around 20% of all global energy is lost to friction: a terrible waste”.

Several big film studios are investing in AI startups or collaborating with new AI studios. Veteran directors including Ron Howard and Paul Schrader are working on AI-enabled films, while a new generation of AI-native film-makers such as Kavan the Kid and Gossip Goblin are using AI to build huge audiences outside the conventional studio system.

Asked whether the real Garbo would have wanted to continue performing as an AI-enabled actor, Reisfield said: “She was at the forefront of cinema in the silent film era. She made the transition to ‘talkies’ and dominated box office receipts.

“So to imagine her as an AI-enabled actor given her track record and ability to captivate and connect with audiences of both men and women isn’t inconceivable.”

Reisfield said the custodians of the rights to Garbo’s voice, name, image and publicity aimed to “preserve, protect, and enhance” her legacy and were “very discerning” on partnerships. Her likeness has been posthumously used by the fashion houses Ferragamo, Gucci and Louis Vuitton but the AI performance for SKF is her first in moving images.

Whatever the future holds for AI Garbo, it kept to the true spirit of the actor by signing off the ball-bearing advert with her immortal line from Grand Hotel: “I want to be alone.”

Entertainment.title: Celebrity Traitors: What you need to know ahead of the first show
Entertainment.text:
The Celebrity Traitors is back for a second series, and viewers will see the likes of Michael Sheen, Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant and Amol Rajan at the round table along with Bella Ramsey, Leigh-Anne Pinnock, Maya Jama and King Kenny.

There are 21 celebrities taking part in total - two more than last year - and there will be an extra episode after the huge popularity of last year's series.

The extended 75-minute debut episode starts at 20:00 BST on Thursday, with Claudia Winkleman again hosting the murderous game.

Viewers can expect some fresh ideas, and executive producer Sarah Fay said they "always want to push the envelope" with the show's elaborate tasks.

"We're always trying to evolve existing ideas to bring them into a new life or coming up with different cultural references," she told the show's press launch.

In the show's trailer, external, they are seen arriving in a church, smiling as they greet each other, but looking nervous.

They later travel to the castle in a fleet of black cars, before Winkleman chooses her traitors while everyone wears their blindfolds.

They then take part in their first mission in a lake in wetsuits, ending with Winkleman saying ominously: "Fame won't save them."

Speaking at the press launch, Winkleman said she is totally focused on the celebrities while she's in the castle, and is glued to the monitors showing footage of them throughout the day.

"All of them were tremendous, and when we do any series I have this room with the monitors. I'm like a weirdo just applying fake tan, watching," she said.

The presenter added that even when she's told to go home, she tells the producers "I am not leaving", joking that she got barely any sleep.

Ed Gamble, host of BBC Two spin-off show Uncloaked, added that he watched "hours of footage a day" as well.

"So when they're eating breakfast, I'm eating breakfast watching them eat breakfast. It's actually quite sad... I'm normally sat there in my pyjamas eating cereal, watching them eat cereal," he told BBC News.

Viewers can also look forward to more of Winkleman's eclectic wardrobe choices.

"I like the fact that it is 'human crow meets golf caddy meets the Artful Dodger'. We're pretty happy with it," she joked about this year's outfits.

The celebrities have also been speaking about the show before its launch, with comedian and presenter Romesh Ranganathan saying that despite being best friends with fellow comic Rob Beckett, he would have no problem stabbing him in the back.

"I mean, he's just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity," he said.

The show's other comics include Joe Lycett, James Acaster and Joanne McNally.

"I think we're going to be the first ones under the magnifying glass being looked at," Acaster said over suspicions one will be a traitor.

Comedian Alan Carr won the first series of Celebrity Traitors, which was the most watched TV programme of 2025 in the UK, watched by 15 million people.

The Last of Us and Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey already has experience of playing similar games at drama clubs and at home, which is why they joined the show.

"I've been playing a version of The Traitors since I was 10 years old," they said.

Mathematician Hannah Fry, who called herself "toxically competitive", added she has already looked for "statistical patterns" in the data for previous games; while Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock said she took advice from singer Cat Burns, who reached the final as a traitor last year.

"She had good advice. She said it might get intense around that round table – but remember, it's just a game," Pinnock said.

The show is also something of a love letter to the Scottish Highlands, where it is filmed, with sweeping drone shots of the scenery and Ardross Castle in Inverness, where the celebrities meet, eat and of course sit at the round table.

"It's breathtaking," Winkleman told the press, adding that she and her family were returning to the Highlands for a holiday.

"My husband was like, 'You're already there quite a lot, what's the matter with you?'" she said.

"It's the most beautiful place I've ever been in the world, is the truth."

After she recently chose to end her recent BBC One chat show, Winkleman is back on familiar ground with Celebrity Traitors.

BBC News asked if she would ever want to try being a contestant on the show, perhaps in the US or Australian versions.

"No, I'm too thick," she said in typical self-deprecating style.

"I mustn't play it in public. I must not.

"I'm just being honest - it's a privilege to play that game and to be at the round table, but I think I would just be too awful at it."

The Celebrity Traitors series two begins on Thursday 1 October at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer. The series will air two nights a week, on Thursday and Friday evenings.

Entertainment.title: Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! presenter, Childline founder and assisted dying campaigner
Entertainment.text:
Dame Esther Rantzen, who has died at the age of 86, was best known for presenting the BBC TV programme That's Life!

Over two decades, what started as a consumer programme with quirky asides became renowned for its high-profile campaigns, notably against child abuse.

It resulted in Dame Esther setting up Childline, a national telephone helpline for children suffering abuse or neglect.

She later became a renowned campaigner for older people and, in the last years of her life, for the legalisation of medically-assisted death.

The final That's Life! was broadcast on 19 June 1994 and featured a look back at both the highlights of the programme and Rantzen's own campaigning.

Possibly the most important and lasting result of any That's Life! campaign was the setting up of Childline in 1986. It followed a number of incidents, featured on the programme, including one in which a toddler had starved to death, locked in a bedroom.

Rantzen persuaded the BBC after the programme was transmitted that a helpline should be set up so that children suffering abuse or neglect could call in confidence. In the 48 hours it was open, it was inundated with calls.

This led to Rantzen campaigning for a 24/7 service to be set up. Childcare professionals claimed it would be impossible but she managed both to raise the money and persuade BT to provide premises and a free phone line.

By the time Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006, it had 12 centres in the UK and the idea was quickly copied in many countries abroad.

Rantzen also went on to make an appearance on the ITV show I'm a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here in 2008.

She wrote a number of regular columns for newspapers and magazines and also involved herself with more than 50 charities.

Following the MPs' expenses scandal in 2009, Rantzen announced she would stand for parliament in Luton South.

She pitched herself against the sitting Labour MP, Margaret Moran, who had claimed expenses in excess of £23,000 for her second home in Southampton.

Moran stood down two days later but Rantzen fought the seat in the 2010 General Election, coming fourth with just over 4% of the vote.

Rantzen was made an OBE in 1991 and CBE in 2006. In the 2015 New Year Honours list, she was appointed a Dame Commander in recognition of the two helpline services she set up.

The following year she warned of the social media pressure on children in the digital world, urging families to "be aware" of the issue.

Speaking on Desert Island Discs in 2019, Dame Esther told presenter Lauren Laverne that her own broadcasting career would not be as successful if she had joined the industry now as a young woman, because she would not be "pretty enough".

In December 2023, Dame Esther said that she was taking a "miracle" treatment for her lung cancer, adding that she might "buzz off to Zurich" - where assisted dying is legal - if it did not work.

A year later, she witnessed the House of Commons vote in favour of the first stage of a Bill that might make a medically-assisted death legal in England and Wales. A similar bill was introduced to the Scottish Parliament.

Although Dame Esther knew that she would not live long enough to take advantage of any new law, she said she wanted to protect other families from "the same agonising experience".

"In the olden days, doctors would ease you out of life and the difference was it wasn't necessarily with your consent," she said.

In March 2025, her daughter confirmed that the drug that had kept Dame Esther alive since her cancer diagnosis was no longer working. They had always known that its effects would be temporary.

Last December, she told a newspaper that she was planning "an 'official' Christmas with my children and five grandchildren, slightly ahead of the real Christmas so that there will be more chance that I am actually alive to enjoy it with them!"

In September 2026, the House of Commons voted against the Assisted Dying Bill, a decision Dame Esther described as "a tragic day".

She added that she was now too frail to travel to Switzerland to end her life.

"Everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now," she said, "which means that the people I love and care about either cannot visit me, or when they do, see me suffering pain or indignity which will inevitably get between them and our shared happy memories, and may even overwhelm the way they think of me."

The broadcaster and campaigner was once asked about what drove her to get involved in a multitude of causes.

"I need to be needed," she said. "It's what makes you get up in the morning, and makes you feel when you go to bed that the day has been well spent.

"There's a real pleasure in feeling somebody needs your help and that you actually have made a difference."

Entertainment.title: Harry and Meghan: Photographer spotted near Archie and Lilibet's school as Sussexes condemn 'reckless intrusion'
Entertainment.text:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have accused an international photographer of "extraordinary recklessness" for looking into the grounds of the school attended by their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

Two men, both wearing backpacks, were spotted circling the perimeter of the school, with police later identifying one of them as an international press photographer.

A spokesman for Prince Harry and Meghan called it "an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children".

Harry, Meghan, and their children returned to the UK last month after living in California for six years.

The BBC understands that the two men were observed by both private security and school staff on Monday morning, stopping at various points and looking into the school grounds, before returning to a van which police later established was a rental vehicle.

One of the men was later identified as photographer for a European press agency.

"The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless," Harry and Meghan's spokesman said.

"There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day."

The spokesman continued: "Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school."

The children began school in the UK at the start of September, but changed after a few days after security concerns were raised about traffic during the school run.

Earlier this month, it emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their move back.

Entertainment.text:

"She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives.

"Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time."

The statement concluded: "If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988."

Chad Lowe, the brother of fellow actor Rob Lowe, won an Emmy Award in 1993 for TV show Life Goes On and has appeared in other programmes including Pretty Little Liars and Supergirl.

He and Painter are also parents to daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, 10.

Entertainment.title: Lady A singer Charles Kelley reveals blood cancer diagnosis
Entertainment.text:
Lady A singer Charles Kelley has revealed he has been diagnosed with blood cancer.

The US musician, 45, founded the Grammy-winning country music trio, previously known as Lady Antebellum, in Nashville in 2006.

The group are known for hits like Need You Now, American Honey and Just a Kiss, and have won six Grammy Awards.

Sharing a health update on Instagram in a video, external alongside his wife Cassie, Kelley announced he had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma - a type of blood cancer that affects the bones and different parts of the body.

He said: "I had a couple of random rib fractures that happened, which sparked my doctor into having me do several different blood tests. And one of the last blood tests we did, they found a blood cancer in there called multiple myeloma, and it's rare."

He added: "But I'm young, I feel healthy, and the treatments I will say have just come so far, even in the past five years. Even life expectancy just far exceeds what it used to be and, I don't know, I feel really hopeful. I really do."

Kelley noted how "freeing" it feels simply "getting this stuff off your chest".

"But we're going to get through it," he continued - comparing his "one day at a time" approach to dealing with cancer to that of his journey to sobriety.

The singer, who shares two young sons with his wife, ended the video by saying he intended to carry on working, despite the diagnosis.

"Right now I feel great and we've got a new record coming out soon with Lady A and then we've got Christmas shows," he said.

"This first six months of treatment I believe is not going to be too invasive. I can still work. I think physically I will feel like myself. I will have tough days, but I want to keep working...

"I need to be happy and doing what I love to do, and spending and soaking up as much time with my family as I can...

"It's just another hurdle and, you know, I feel confident that we're going to get through it."

Kelley's bandmates Hillary Scott and Dave Haywood posted messages of support for him and his family in the comments.

Fellow lead vocalist Scott wrote: "The strongest duo right there! Love y'all so much! You've got this!"

Haywood added: "Covering you in prayer brother. Love y'all. We're all here for you!"

The group have had three number one albums in the US and reached number two with their single Need You Now, which won record of the year and song of the year at the Grammys in 2011.

Entertainment.title: Oasis unheard recordings pulled from auction after band 'sue'
Entertainment.text:
A set of unheard Oasis recordings valued at between £1.2m and £1.6m have been pulled from an auction after the band filed an injunction.

Earlier this month, it was announced that Littleton Auctions, in Evesham, were selling a set of recordings which included 63 live shows, as well as soundchecks and more than 100 hours of Noel and Liam Gallagher in the 1990s.

They were collected by Oasis sound engineer Huw Richards, who worked with the band from the release of their debut album Definitely, Maybe in 1994, until 2001.

However, the auction house said the sale of the recordings had been suspended after the band intervened.

Managing director Ben Homer said: "Littleton Auctions confirms that the Oasis recordings known as The Desk Tapes have been withdrawn from our October 3 auction in light of legal proceedings.

"We are very disappointed that we cannot offer this significant archive as planned."

Entertainment.title: Lola Young: Vaping making it harder to breathe, singer says
Entertainment.text:
Singer Lola Young has said her breathing feels like a "chore" due to the effects of vaping.

In a TikTok video,, external the Grammy winner told her followers her lungs feel "battery powered".

The 25-year-old has previously acknowledged in videos she "should quit", but suggested in her latest post that is unlikely to happen any time soon.

Vocal coach Lizzii Hills has told BBC Newsbeat vaping is "not advised" for artists and that difficulty breathing can affect a singer's voice and performance.

"Somebody once said to me, 'Lola there will be a day when you wake up, you'll be 25 or 26, from a deep sleep, and you'll start to feel the effects of vaping'," the Messy singer said in her post.

"You know what I said? I said 'nah' and rolled my eyes.

"But let me tell you something, the day has come."

Last month, The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) linked vaping to higher rates of breathing problems after reviewing more than 80 studies.

The review also found an association with wheezing, coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Describing her symptoms, Young said: "My lungs feel like they're battery powered, like they're just one big battery.

"Breathing feels like a chore, it feels like hard work, it feels like I should be paid for breathing. It feels like there will be no tomorrow."

The NHS says vaping is less harmful than smoking, external, but notes there are still risks - many of which are still not known.

The government is introducing measures to make vapes less attractive, including a ban on single-use vapes, introduced last year.

And from Thursday a new tax will be applied to e-cigarette liquid, with an additional £2.20 added per 10ml.

Hills, who helps artists with their vocals, says vaping can have an impact on an artist's voice and struggling to breathe can risk straining your voice.

"Vaping may not affect the voice box just itself, it affects the lungs, the airways, the throat - it's all respiratory, it's all connected. So doing that can affect your vocal technique," she says.

"Breathing is really important. Singing requires controlled inhalation and sustained, efficient exhalation.

"You end up trying harder, putting in more effort for the same results you were getting beforehand."

She adds that when artists struggle with their voice, it can have significant psychological impacts on them too.

"They can feel like they've lost themselves," she says. "It can become quite a big deal emotionally."

Overall, she wouldn't recommend vaping to her clients.

"As a performer, as an artist, you want to stay in the best health you can for your voice to work at its best.

"We all know it's not the healthy choice and if you can avoid it - absolutely."

Young returned to the spotlight earlier this year following a five-month hiatus after she collapsed on stage.

She has been open in the past about her struggles with her health and addiction, previously telling The Guardian, external about dealing with cocaine dependency.

She has also struggled with her mental health and was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and ADHD when she was a teenager.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted Young's representatives for comment.

Entertainment.title: Tapestry tour will include audio-described guide for blind people
Entertainment.text:
The British Museum will provide an audio-described tour of the Bayeux Tapestry after a man with visual impairment pointed out the lack of access for blind and partially-sighted people.

Dr Yusuf Ali Osman, from Croydon, said the museum breached the Equality Act by not offering such tours of the exhibition.

On Wednesday, the central London museum said an in-person audio-described tour would be held during the exhibition's run.

It said it was also exploring adding an audio-described tour to the exhibition's app.

Osman, who has no sight in either eye, contacted the museum via solicitor Leigh Day to ask whether audio-described tours would be available.

The law firm told him the museum had said self-guided visits would be prioritised over tours and events.

The British Museum said this was because there are limits on how many hours of light to which the tapestry can be exposed - and this in turn restricted visitor numbers.

Osman is seeking damages and a declaration that he was discriminated against and an order requiring the museum to change its policies.

He also said relevant staff should be given disability awareness training and he hoped the legal action would "help make sure blind and partially sighted people are properly considered" when major exhibitions are planned.

His solicitor said the Equality Act placed obligations on service providers to anticipate the needs of disabled people and take reasonable steps to avoid substantial disadvantage.

"Our client is asking for the same opportunity as sighted visitors to experience this exhibition."

A British Museum spokesperson said the museum was "committed to making the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition as accessible as possible" and had worked with specialist access consultants.

Provisions currently include a sensory map to help visitors prepare for their visit, as well as dedicated tours during the exhibition run which will include an in-person audio-described tour, the spokesperson said.

"We are also exploring including a separate audio-described tour as part of the exhibition's app-based audio guide."

The 70m (230ft) embroidery, which depicts the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of 1066, is on loan from France and is on display at the museum until 11 July 2027.

Entertainment.title: First Glastonbury Festival 2027 tickets to go on sale
Entertainment.text:
Those hoping to go to Glastonbury Festival 2027 could soon find out their fate as the first set of tickets go on sale.

The event will take place from 23-27 June 2027 at Worthy Farm in Pilton, Somerset, after a fallow year in 2026.

Coach tickets will be available to buy for £408 plus the selected coach fare at 18:00 BST on Thursday, before general admission tickets go on sale at 09:00 on Sunday.

Coaches will depart from 28 locations across the country including from London, Bristol, Bath, Glasgow, Edinburgh, Manchester and Cardiff.

People who want to snag a ticket must have already pre-registered on the Glastonbury Festival website.

In recent years, organisers have introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

Registration closed on 25 September, and will not reopen until after the October ticket sales.

Once on the other side of the queue, people can buy up to six tickets per transaction after paying a deposit.

Anyone who missed the registration deadline or is not able to buy a ticket on Thursday can have another chance during the spring resale.

Entertainment.title: EastEnders actor Shane Richie banned from driving after speeding
Entertainment.text:
EastEnders actor Shane Richie blamed "baiting" from paparazzi as he was banned from driving for six months after being caught speeding.

Court records revealed the 62-year-old, real name Shane Roche, was hit with the driving ban on 23 September after he admitted the offence in Reigate, Surrey.

He was also fined £500 at Guildford Magistrates' Court and ordered to pay £320 in costs and a surcharge.

Richie, best known for playing Alfie Moon in the BBC soap, is already awaiting trial over a separate alleged offence of drink-driving in Harlow, Essex.

In a note to the court, regarding the speeding offence, Richie said he had been pursued daily by photographers due to his "very public divorce".

The actor accused the press of "constantly baiting me" for months in an attempt to get an angry reaction on camera.

"This is not an excuse for going five miles over the limit, but just a reason why I may have sped up on that particular road," he said.

Richie was caught on camera driving a Ford at 35mph (56km/h) along Reigate Hill - which is a steep climb leading to and from the nearby M25 junction - on 15 March.

In his note to the court, Richie apologised for the offence and said: "Over the past several months I've been followed from my place of work in Borehamwood (Hertfordshire) where I film sometimes six days a week by our British tabloid press…. to my home."

He described being followed into Reigate and to the supermarket.

"It's no secret now that I'm going through a very public divorce and for the last several months the British press have suspected this and have been constantly baiting me and almost always looking for a reaction from me to sell their newspapers," Richie added.

Entertainment.title: Danni from Dorset becomes first contestant to leave Bake Off
Entertainment.text:
An HGV service administrator from Dorset has become the first person to leave this year's Great British Bake Off.

Danni was eliminated from the Channel 4 TV series during biscuit week after being told by judge Paul Hollywood their cookies were "powdery".

During the episode, which aired on Tuesday, Danni said they had been unable to taste the cookies because the ingredients included cream and butter and they were vegan.

They said competing on Bake Off gave them "some of the best advice about how to improve something that I love".

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent's Dorset Breakfast show, they said: "It was absolutely fantastic, on and off camera. I was just hyped to be there.

"Some of my favourite parts were the technicals which I was consistently not great on doing but I loved doing them so much... It's like a puzzle."

Reflecting on their time in the tent, Danni said: "I've never been the best with making friends.

"I'm quite an eccentric person and quite a Marmite person.

"Going into it, I wasn't expecting to make friends. I wasn't expecting there to be so many lovely, lovely people.

"It wasn't a competitive environment at all, it's just a bit of fun you are having with your friends."

Hairdresser Tom, from West Yorkshire, was named star baker on Tuesday.

During the episode, bakers made American-style cookies, recreated iced gems and created a "visually striking" biscuit mosaic.

Entertainment.title: Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86
Entertainment.text:
Esther Rantzen, the Bafta-winning TV presenter and founder of Childline, has died aged 86.

In a statement, her family paid tribute to “the most wonderful mother” and “cherished grandmother”, whose “legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her”.

“We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably. She was our sunshine. We will always remember her endless capacity for joy, her ability to comfort every heartache, her beautiful way with words and her expert guidance in all things,” said her three children.

Rantzen announced a diagnosis of stage four lung cancer in 2023, and became a vocal campaigner to change the law around assisted dying. In September 2026, she announced she had to abandon plans to end her life in Swiss clinic Dignitas, due to being too physically frail.

“Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful; indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest,” she said in a statement. “And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.”

“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Very sad to hear that Dame Esther Rantzen has died. Through her decades of campaigning, including founding Childline and The Silver Line, she changed countless lives and gave a voice to people who often went unheard.

“And I will always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life. My thoughts are with her family and all who loved her.”

Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced a bill to legalise assisted dying, said: “Esther was a strong, warm and compassionate woman and a fighter to the end.

“Her positivity and determination never to give in gave me strength, but more importantly helped all those others like her who were confronting a terminal illness to keep going in the knowledge that they were not alone.”

Rantzen was born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire, in 1940 and began her career in 1963 as a BBC radio studio manager. Having moved into television as a researcher, she became a presenter in 1968, as part of the consumer affairs show Braden’s Week, before being appointed as the main host of its replacement programme, That’s Life!, in 1973.

Part magazine, part consumer show, with hard-hitting investigations and jokes, That’s Life! drew more than 20 million viewers at its peak – and ran for 21 years with Rantzen as anchor. After she successfully pitched an episode about child abuse to the then BBC controller Michael Grade, a set of phone lines was opened for 48 hours, which enabled children to call in and speak to social workers. The volume of responses led her to turn the service into a permanent fixture, launching the children’s charity Childline in 1986.

In 1988, Rantzen created Hearts of Gold, a series focusing on people responsible for outstanding acts of kindness, and hosted her own BBC Two chatshow, Esther, from 1994, when That’s Life! came to an end, until 2002. Further TV projects included the consumer affairs show Old Dogs New Tricks, as well as competing in Strictly Come Dancing’s second series and the 2008 edition of the ITV reality show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! She received an OBE for services to broadcasting, Bafta’s Richard Dimbleby award for factual programming and a lifetime achievement prize at the Women in Film and Television awards.

Her wide-ranging charity work saw her act as a patron or vice-president of numerous organisations. In 2010, she launched the Silver Line – a free confidential helpline for older people, which led to her being made a dame for services to children and older people.

In 2010, she stood as an independent candidate for Luton South in that year’s general election, coming fourth after winning 4.4% of the vote. She wrote numerous books, including a murder-mystery novel. In later years, she was a regular contributor to the One Show and hosted a podcast with her former That’s Life! colleague Adrian Mills.

On Instagram, the television presenter Anna Williamson described Rantzen as “somebody truly iconic, who really cared, and who has left behind one hell of a legacy”.

Fellow presenter Lorraine Kelly also paid tribute to Rantzen on social media for being a “pioneer and a force of nature – [who] helped so many people – funny, forthright and fabulous”.

One of Rantzen’s former co-hosts of That’s Life!, Howard Leader, said: “Over the time that I was with her, through her fantastic generosity, she taught me how to be a journalist.

“I think Esther’s skill was that she really understood how to use the platform she had to create an effect for, we hope ... the improvement of people in our country.”

Her husband, Desmond Wilcox, whom she married in 1977, died in 2000. Rantzen is survived by their three children, Miriam, Rebecca and Joshua – as well as five grandchildren.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike taken to hospital after attempted execution, lawyer says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after her heart was still beating following two lethal injections during her execution, her lawyer says.

Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening, saying: "Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring."

One of her attorneys told the BBC that Pike, 50, was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital after two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered.

There has been no comment yet from the state of Tennessee. Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

The attempted execution took place at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville at about 20:00 local time on Wednesday night.

Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital, and the curtain in the witness room was closed twice, the Associated Press reports.

Media were at some point asked to leave, the news agency said.

Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper: "Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution.

"We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion to stay her execution and administer medical care after the lethal injection was apparently botched.

District Judge Clifton L Corker issued a ruling noting that "medical personnel have begun to administer medical care as requested in the motion".

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she likely never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure during the attempted execution.

"It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury," Zivot said in an email.

The capital punishment went ahead after the US Supreme Court overturned a reprieve granted by a lower court on Wednesday morning. It was the second time in as many days that the justices gave the go-ahead for Pike's death by lethal injection.

In a ruling earlier in the day, judges from the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit paused the execution saying they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.

Her lawyers had argued the jury did not get the chance to weigh mitigating evidence of Pike's documented history of childhood sexual abuse, before they sentenced her to death in 1996.

The defence said that for years, the state of Tennessee had argued in court that she lied about being sexually abused as a child.

But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute that she had suffered sexual abuse and rape.

Tennessee's governor denied a clemency request this week from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

In her clemency petition, Pike said that she intended to beat Slemmer, not kill her, but that she was unable to "put the brakes on".

"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid," she said in a statement. "It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."

The murder in 1995 created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee, after Colleen was found with an inverted pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the symbol herself.

Before the killing, Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend.

Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.

Colleen Slemmer's mother had said she wanted the execution to take place, telling the Associated Press she had waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.

"Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," May Martinez told the agency on Saturday.

She said a group helped raise funds for her and her husband to travel from Florida to Tennessee to witness the execution.

"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said.

Since 1976, when the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty, only 18 women have been executed in the US, compared to 1,663 men. That's about 1% of all US executions.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Dame Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Dame Esther Rantzen, who presented BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the charity Childline, has died at the age of 86.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the veteran broadcaster and campaigner had "changed countless lives".

Dame Esther hosted and produced That's Life! during its run from 1973 to 1994. It regularly attracted 20 million viewers for its mixture of serious consumer investigations and light-hearted items.

She launched Childline, a British counselling service for children and young people, in 1986, and in 2013 she launched Silver Line to help elderly people suffering from isolation and loneliness. Later in life, she became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.

She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In December 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic.

But in a statement given to the Press Association earlier this month, she said that despite having "spent the money and made the plans" to go to Dignitas, she had since reached the point where she was "too physically fragile to make the journey".

She added that the law must "change and change quickly", as she renewed her plea ahead of the latest debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, which failed to pass through the Commons.

Rantzen joined BBC radio as a sound effects assistant before becoming a TV researcher, and in 1968 she trained as a producer and director.

The young broadcaster became a researcher and reporter for Bernard Braden's consumer affairs programme, Braden's Week.

When That's Life! launched in 1973, she was its figurehead and became a popular fixture on screens as the show's formidable and fun-loving presenter and producer.

The consumer show's notable items, according to her website, external, included "talking dogs, Jobsworth Awards and campaigns on behalf of abused children, organ transplants, safe playgrounds, and to provide justice for consumers".

Its most-viewed episode featured Sir Nicholas Winton being introduced for the first time to survivors he had saved from the Holocaust, during a 1988 instalment of the show.

Later in her career, she also appeared on Strictly Come Dancing, First Dates and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here!

Dame Esther was married to documentary film-maker Desmond Wilcox from 1977 until he died in 2000. They had three children.

She was made a dame in 2015 for her services to children and older people.

Dame Esther went on to become a vocal campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.

In December 2024, she spoke of her "great relief" after MPs backed proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, before they ultimately stalled in the House of Lords.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, external in November 2025, before the bill ran out of time, she said that "as long as others in the future will be able to ask for help to die as they choose, I will die happy".

She expressed her disappointment after MPs voted against a fresh attempt to introduce the legislation in September. Some disability campaigners described the result as a "victory", while Dame Esther said it was "deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it".

"I am sure a change in the law will come," she added.

Figures from politics, broadcasting and the charity sector have paid tribute to Dame Esther for her impact on public life.

The prime minister said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life".

BBC director-general Matt Brittin paid tribute to Dame Esther as a "legend of British broadcasting" whose contribution to public life was "immeasurable".

"Her warmth, spirit and fight for justice and action that we saw on our screens continued long after the programme ended, with a lifetime of campaigning where she changed the lives of millions," he said.

Fellow broadcaster and money saving expert Martin Lewis called Dame Esther an "inspiration" and a "pioneer" whose "impact and memory will long continue to shine".

Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners.

Chris Sherwood, the chief executive of the NSPCC, which runs the Childline helpline, said Dame Esther had gone to "exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help".

Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning.

"She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said.

Anton Du Beke, Dame Esther's partner on Strictly Come Dancing, shared a photo of the pair dancing together in the 2004 series, writing that the two had "remained firm friends" ever since.

He praised her "breadth of knowledge and passion" and called her "the ultimate breaker of the glass ceiling", adding: "She will be greatly missed and my sincere thoughts are with her family."

Presenter Timmy Mallet, who starred in a series of I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here! alongside Dame Esther, said he was thinking of her after they had "shared the jungle together".

He captioned a collection of photos of the pair: "God bless you Esther".

Davina McCall wrote on Instagram that Dame Esther had "made the world a better place, and inspired so many of us to do better and live life to its fullest."

The message accompanied a video of the former Big Brother host discussing how Dame Esther was an "inspiration to girls like me when we were growing up".

Presenter Amol Rajan said Dame Esther "changed the course of millions of lives" as he paid tribute, calling her "an inspirational, strong woman ahead of her time".

"Not bad for a bright, Hertfordshire girl born during the early stages of the Second World War."

Watch Katie Razzall's half-hour special programme Esther! on iPlayer. It will also be shown this Friday, 2 October, on BBC One at 19:30 BST.
